utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. May we please hear the case number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And the appearances of today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Nicholas Koumjian with Ruth Karper for the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic, John Ostojic, and Danilo Cirkovic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I take the opportunity after this long break to ask Dr. Stakic himself about his health condition and are there any problems regarding the conditions in the Detention Unit?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. At the moment, I'm in good health, and I have no particular objections to make regarding the conditions in the Detention Unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated again. You may be advised that no doubt the same rules apply as they did since the beginning of this case, that it's your right to address this Bench whenever, after having contacted your Defence counsel, this Bench, and especially when you feel it appropriate to intervene, be it in the form as foreseen under our rules as a formal witness, or by an own statement also in the framework of our rules. You may have seen, and this is true for both parties, that we have to a certain extent an enlarged time frame. I think it's helpful that we can start all the days from now on until the end of the Prosecutor's case in the morning, and have additional the afternoon. Even though it may be possible that the one or other day has to be cancelled, no doubt, it's time enough to close the Prosecutor's case. Until then, and if there is no unforeseeable real obstacle, the case of the Prosecutor has to be finalised as scheduled. This is Thursday, the 19th September. If there should be the one or other obstacle, please discuss this as soon as possible. And the Judges want to ask the Prosecutor to concentrate during the rest of the Prosecutor's case, first of all, on questions related, no doubt, you know it yourself, related to the personal responsibility to link to those events shown in the past to Dr. Stakic, but also to the question why - we mentioned this earlier - why this special time limit, why starting at this period in time, why ending at that period of time, and here it could be indeed, and the Defence should think about this issue very carefully, whether it's appropriate to present Dr. Stakic either as a witness or in the form of a statement as regard the end of the alleged activities in 1992. And it's, of course for the Prosecutor to describe and to declare why they held, necessary to limit the case for this short period, relatively short period of time. One issue remaining, having reviewed that what has been said since April here in this courtroom is no doubt the question of the mens rea, the state of mind, especially as regards the intent. And there is no doubt the burden of proof for the Prosecutor, and we have, first of all, to rely on certain documents. But it could be also helpful for the Defence already during the presentation of the Prosecution's case give their own presentation or give the presentation through the words of Dr. Stakic in order to limitate as far as possible the case after the end of said case of the Prosecution. And it's not for nothing that you will find after the -- immediately after the close of the Prosecution's case some days called deliberations or negotiations, and this is the attempt really to streamline the case both on the factual basis as well as on the -- as regards the charges. Both is important, and both is indispensable because in relation to other cases, be it in the framework of this Tribunal, be it in the comparison to cases on domestic level, for me, it seems to be scandalous that our case should take us more than one year. It is necessary for all participants to streamline this case. Having said this, I want to ask the Prosecution to concentrate during this week, first of all, on the witnesses summoned from abroad. Maybe we should hear, and we can hear in-house witnesses later. Admittedly, there are some reasons during this week endangering the continuity of the case. I'll try to do my very best, but I can't guarantee that I can be here all the time. Probably we have to make use of Rule 15 bis. But I regard it as necessary to hear at least the witnesses called from abroad. If there is no other special intervention, then we could immediately start with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Just before the witness is brought in, the witness requested this morning a pseudonym.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Pseudonym. Objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask, after this long period of time, Madam Registrar, what will be the next available pseudonym? Did we have already W? So it would be Witness X. Could the usher please bring in Witness X.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness X. Can you hear me in a language you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I can hear you in a language I can understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And please understand, in addition, that we will call you, for your own protection as "Witness X," and not call you with your own name. It's for your own protection. It's not to be unpolite. Do you understand? May we please hear your solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Witness X, please be seated. And the Office of the Prosecutor may start, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Examined by Mr. Koumjian:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness X. Can you tell the Court the year that you were born.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I was born (redacted) .

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, can the day and month be redacted from the transcript?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I ask --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No objections? May the day and month of the birth be redacted, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness X, where were you born?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I was born in Prijedor Municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you grow up?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I grew up in the village of Biscani, Prijedor Municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you educated in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, I was. I went to elementary school and secondary school in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I am a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to take you to 1991. At that time, where were you living at the beginning of 1991?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: At the beginning of 1991, I was living in Biscani. However, I also spent some time in that period in Sarajevo at the police academy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going to where in Biscani -- did you live with your parents?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes. I lived in the same house with my father, my mother, and my sister.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you spent some time at the police academy in Sarajevo. Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes. That was a police academy, a four-year programme. But I came to Sarajevo in 1991, and I stayed there until April 1992 when the war began. When the war began in 1992, I left the academy and returned to my home municipality, Prijedor Municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you actually in training -- before April 1992, were you actually being trained as a police officer? Were you a cadet? You have to answer out loud. Sorry, I didn't hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I was a cadet between 1991 and April 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In April 1992 when the conflict began in Bosnia, what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: In April 1992, I was working in a department at the academy. It was part of the main police academy in Sarajevo in a place called Tarcin. That's where I was when the war began, when the conflict began and when the barricades were set up in Sarajevo. I was there at that school. And we were told that the school was being closed and that we should all do as we saw fit, and perhaps go to our homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do? Did you go back to your home?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, we did that. And the school was dissolved. There was an order -- an order was issued for the school to close, and we returned home to northwest Bosnia. The school was in Central Bosnia, near Sarajevo. We left on our own initiatives in a manner of speaking with our fellow students from the school who knew the area, and they were our guides actually. They took us through the surrounding mountains and villages until we reached our final destination.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The other cadets at the academy that you studied with, were they of one particular nationality or different nationalities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: They were of different nationalities. There were Muslim, Croat, and Serb cadets. It was a mixed group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So did you return to Biscani in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I returned to Biscani, my place of birth.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall anything about the 30th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The 30th of April, 1992, Serbs took the police -- the Prijedor Police Station by force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did things change at all for the people of Biscani after that takeover?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, a lot changed. We were isolated. We were cut off. We had no access to the town, and we lived in some sort of an enclave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your father's occupation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: He was a joiner by profession and a construction worker also.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your father able to work after the takeover?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: No, no one was, not my father, not any of the other Muslims there. They were all dismissed from their jobs. And they couldn't go to the town. There were checkpoints being set up all around the town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the people of Biscani set up their own checkpoint or organise any kind of defence or patrols?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Not at that time, nothing in particular. Just at night, we would simply go outside our own houses and guard our own families from anything happening to them. But there was nothing special aside from that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall an incident happening in Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, there was an incident in Hambarine about 20 days after Prijedor Municipality was stormed by the Serb authorities. On the 22nd of May, there was an incident. A checkpoint had been set up there already, and people started organising themselves. That was some kind of self-defence, they were watching the roads leading into the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we have S170 put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Witness X, the diagram that's on the screen is also to your right. Perhaps you could take a pointer and just point on the diagram to your right where your village that you were living in, Biscani, was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The village of Biscani was right here, the blue dot on the map here west of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Indicating the blue dot just south of Ravine and just to the east of Mrkalj.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that correct? That's where you lived at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've also talked about Hambarine. Can you point to where that is on the map?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Hambarine are further south, south of Biscani. This point on the map.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were Hambarine and Biscani both in an area called Brdo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you show us which area is Brdo? Can you circle that area with your -- with the pointer and tell us where it is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: On the map, I'll circle it like this, just follow the movement of my pen. South of Hambarine, there's the village of Zecovi. That's so to speak the southern most point in Brdo. And then it stretches all the way to the River Sana in the valley, and then up to Ravine at the northernmost point, and on to Alagici and further on south to Zecovi. So this would be the circle.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And I believe, is it correct, that in that circle you indicated that Carakovo was within the boundaries of the Brdo area on the eastern part? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Where was the barricade for Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The barricade for Hambarine was at the road we used to refer to as the Ljubija Road, because there was a road leading from Prijedor to Ljubija, and that's where the checkpoint was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. How did you hear about the incident at Hambarine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Well, I heard it in this way: On that day when the incident happened, there were people on motorcycles that road very fast on the road through all the surrounding villages, and they told us to hide and to seek shelter because we would be attacked because there was an incident that happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that incident, did you hear any announcements on the radio? Did you ever hear anything communicated by authorities from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: We listened to the Prijedor radio at that time, and the radio spoke to us, to the population, told us to surrender ourselves, or rather that the people who were responsible for the incident should surrender, that is, the checkpoint commander, Aziz Aliskovic, that we should surrender. If he didn't surrender, then he said that we would be attacked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall in whose name this announcement was made? What is your best recollection?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Could you put your question a little more simply, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll try. Do you recall who made that order, that order was made on whose behalf that Aziz Aliskovic had to be surrendered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: It was issued by the Crisis Staff or someone in -- certainly by the Serb authorities. They issued the order because they had the control of all the main points. On the 30th of April, the 1st of May when the police station was taken, all the crucial facilities were taken, and everything was in their hands, in the Serb hands.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that order, ultimatum, was given, was the Brdo area attacked?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: On that night, they fired four shells, and then it was probably that the group hadn't surrendered, the people who were sought did not surrender. And on that night, they fired four shells on Hambarine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was the night of the 22nd, or the morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, between 22nd and 23rd of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened on the 23rd of May?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: So the next day, after the shelling, by noon, 1200 hours noon, the Prijedor radio kept broadcasting information that Aziz Aliskovic to surrender with his group, and the ultimatum was by 1200 hours noon. They said that if he didn't surrender, then we would be shelled. The shelling began a few minutes after 12.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you during the shelling?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I was with my family at home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the map that we were just looking at, Biscani appears to be in the northern part of Brdo and Hambarine in the south. Did the shelling reach all the way to Biscani, or where was it concentrated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: It was directed -- the fire was mostly directed at Hambarine, but you already mentioned the Brdo area, and the Brdo was surrounded from all sides with the villages, with nationality, population of Serb nationality. So we were completely surrounded. Mostly Hambarine was shelled, but there were shells going from Hambarine, Rizvanovici, and all over.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was any part of Brdo occupied? Did the army go into any part of Brdo that day or the next day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: On that day, the army took Hambarine because from Prijedor, they started to go with armoured units and with infantry, and they managed to get to Hambarine and to take the highest elevation point because Hambarine is probably the highest elevation point on Brdo. They took the school, and they also made their checkpoint there. And all the population fled to the surrounding villages, to Rizvanovici, and to Biscani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I'd like to talk about a time period from that point until the 20th of July. During that time period, after the attack on Hambarine on the Brdo area until the 20th of July, what was life like in Biscani?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Life was difficult. We were isolated still although we all believed that nothing would happen to us and that people would go back to their homes. But it didn't come to pass. We were isolated in that period, and they asked for all the weapons owned by people to be handed over, all the weapons they had including rifles, handguns, and also the uniforms that people had. Because all the people, regardless of nationality, people had obligations towards the army as reserves, and following their military service, most of the people had uniforms at home still. So all the uniforms and all the weapons were gathered in front of each local community from Biscani up to Rizvanovici, and all this was taken to the barracks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you yourself have a weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I did not have any weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did the people of Biscani agree to give up all their weapons and all of their means of defending themselves?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Simply we believed them that they wouldn't do anything to us, and we thought that if we did it in a nice way, that they wouldn't attack us. That was in that sense. People were afraid.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the events of the 20th of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember the events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in Biscani that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I was throughout this time in Biscani with my family.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your father, mother, and sister?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, my father, mother, and sister, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened that morning, the 20th of July, in Biscani?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: On the 20th of July, there was ethnic cleansing that took place of the entire region of Brdo, not only Biscani but the entire area of Brdo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you see and experience? Tell the Judges what your experience was that day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: That day, in the morning, about 10.00 in the morning, there were shots that were heard from the direction of Prijedor, and we saw that there was burning. There was smoke coming. We saw that houses were being set on fire, but I had no idea what was going on, in fact. And we supposedly heard that there would be a search carried out of houses by the Serb authorities, that they would be searching the houses looking for weapons, and people who didn't hand over their weapons. And people who were in connection with the SDA party, they were mostly sought. So that was the idea we had of a search that was going to be carried out. However, the army was coming from the direction of Prijedor, from the direction specifically of Tukovi, and behind our backs where Cikote and Volar were, the Serb villages and Brezicani, that's where Serbs were also. And they were firing on us so we wouldn't be able to flee there when the other soldiers were coming from the town. So that there would be no resistance. But we were waiting in our homes. We were waiting for the army in our homes, and we thought that they would take us to a football pitch or something like that. And so my father and I were in front of our house when two soldiers came in front of our house, and they told us to go down the road, to go down the village, to go down through the village towards Prijedor. This was a road that was leading to Prijedor. And we were there. There was a coffee bar there. It was a sort of collection point they made there, the Serb soldiers made it so. This is where the people were gathered. This was one of the collecting points. There were several such points in the village. As the army was coming more and more into the village, they were making more of these collecting points but I didn't see these horrific events because I was taken -- I was forced away from my home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about your mother and your sister? Did they go with you and your father?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: No. Nobody, none of the women went. None of the women were sent away from home. They all stayed at home for a while. Only the men, according to their assessment, from 16, 17 onwards, until elderly people, those men were being sent out of their homes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we go on to talk about what happened with you and your father, can you tell us, did you later see your sister and your mother?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Later on, we met in the Trnopolje camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they tell you how they got -- sorry. Did they tell you how they got to the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, we managed to speak a little. It wasn't for very long because they had to go. There was a convoy from Trnopolje which was going to go to Travnik or towards Travnik. But we managed to get some information from them about how they survived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did they survive?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: They were mistreated many times every day the soldiers would force their way into the house every day asking for valuables, gold, money. Then they mistreated my sister a great deal. They found my fisherman's equipment. I used to be a fisherman. And that's why they mistreated her more. I don't particularly know why.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did your sister and mother go on their own to Trnopolje camp or did someone take them there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Nobody went. Everything was done on the initiative of the soldiers who continued to cleanse and loot the villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The soldiers that you saw in Biscani in the Brdo area on the 20th of July, or the men that you saw in uniform, could you tell were they army, police, paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: There were uniforms of all kinds, from all kinds of formations, units. There was olive drab. There was camouflage. There were police uniforms, all kinds of uniforms were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to you and your father? What was your experience after being taken to the collection point by the cafe bar?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: On that collection point, we were there, and we were stopped there for a while because people were being collected at that point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you see there and what happened to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: There, I saw the killings of several people. I saw when people were being tortured, beaten. I saw people being killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us what you remember seeing that day.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I remember that I saw a man who was lying by the roadside, probably dead, probably killed. And I remember that behind the column that were standing there, a column of people where I was as well, when a soldier in uniform called out two men to come out and take this dead man behind a house, and he escorted them behind the house. And then he fired into them, and these two men never returned. I also remember --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you and ask you, the incident that you just told us about, do you remember the names of the people that you saw killed in that incident, either the man that was dead or the two who were taken out to bury him and never returned?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, I remember the names. The person that I thought that was dead, his name was Hamdija Fikic, and the two people who were called out from the group of people where I stood were Mirhad Mrkalj, and Ferid Sabanovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you ever seen any of these three since that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What else happened that you saw?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I also saw when from the very same group they took out a person called Mirhad Mrkalj, a person who used to be a policeman before the war. One of the men recognised him and addressed him as in a way "Mrkalj, do you remember when you took my driving license away"? So he took him out of the group. He started beating him in front of us. Then two of them joined him as well because this man was rather large. He was being beaten there for a while, and then this person took Mirhad behind the cafe bar, and Mirhad did not come back. Afterwards, when Mirhad's wife came to Trnopolje, told me that she found Mirhad with his throat cut behind the cafe bar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know someone named Mirsad Medic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see Mirsad Medic that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, I saw Mirsad, and Mirsad was also taken out on that day during the cleansing. There was Mirsad's colleague who was there. They used to work together at that petrol station. This person's name was Zolka. I'm not sure what his last name was. He took his former colleague, and took him and killed him. And I also saw when another policeman was killed, Sasa Karagic on the very same point, the very same place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to Sasa Karagic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: He was also killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened -- how long were you and your father at the cafe bar collection point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I can't tell you exactly, but I think we were there certainly an hour, perhaps more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Please, go on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's more important for you to finish. Did you finish or have something to add?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I just wanted to mention that while I was standing there in that group of people waiting, not knowing what would happen to us, I recognised a man from Sarajevo who used to be with me in the same dormitory in the school, in the academy. A colleague who arrived in a police car, and he came along and looking at the column as it was by the roadside, and he was looking at faces, and he stopped by me and he recognised me immediately. And he asked me,he addressed me by my last name, and said "(redacted), what are you doing here?" We were all standing with our hands like this, all the time we were standing in a line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that be redacted. Line 20, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can you indicate at least the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: The name, the name of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, please, redact the name of the witness.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but you just mentioned a name that we had to take out of the transcript and the tape, and we can do that if you make a mistake. Don't worry about it. But you're saying that this policeman you knew from the academy came and asked you what you were doing there. What happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, he recognised me and said that I should stay there, and that he would return and save me. However, very quickly after he left, because he left, he continued on with the car, I don't know where he went, the person who was the commander of that collection point, the person who was in uniform, he was dressed in olive drab uniform, and he had a helmet on his head. He wore sort of a Lennon-type dark glasses and he had black mittens of letter [as interpreted] on his hands and he had automatic weapons with him. He had a semi-automatic machine-gun. He called me out from the line, and he asked me: "How come I knew Dragan -- this person who was at school with me? So how come I know Dragan?" So I said we were friends from school. I didn't dare say we were at the police academy together because I was already aware that people who had such background or such positions would simply be killed very quickly. So that's all I said. I said it very briefly. I gave a short answer. And he said he was going to save me, and then he said -- told me to go back to the line, which is what I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the person you knew from Sarajevo, the policeman, also from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: He lived in the village of Svodna. This village was located between Prijedor and Bosanski Novi, about 10 kilometres from Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you were sent back into the line, what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: After I returned to where I was, a bus came. It was Autotransport coach from Prijedor. This bus arrived, and the same person who called me out, who came out of the line, the same person who was in this good uniform and well camouflaged, hiding his face, in my assessment, the line was longer than 100 metres of people on this collection point. And he simply halfed the line next to me. I had a yellow T-shirt on me. I remember it well. And then he said: "Yellow T-shirt and everyone else behind him, we should get on to the bus. And all the others in front of me, they stayed for a while." So we got on to the bus, and we set off to an unknown destination which was -- ended up being Prijedor, or it was towards Prijedor we were going.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During that bus ride, did you see -- did you ever get a chance to look out the window and see anything alongside the road?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: For a few moments, I was curious, and I was a little deeper into the bus, further back in the bus, so a couple of times I look out the window of the bus to see where we were. But then I could see a lot of people lining the road dead. They were lying dead, and there was smoke coming from houses and houses that were burnt. But everybody who was by the driver, or there was a person, a kind of escort standing by the driver driver, we were not supposed to look and we were ordered to keep our heads bent.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did the bus go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The bus went towards Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you stop?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: When we went into Prijedor town itself, and near the police station in Prijedor, I don't know why, perhaps for technical reasons, perhaps the bus wasn't working any more, we changed bus. We went into another bus. It was with the same coach company, also Autotransport Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did this bus take you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: This bus took us on to the Banja Luka Road, so that was Prijedor/Banja Luka Road. That's the road we took. And we were then stopped near Keraterm, at the checkpoint. I saw the checkpoint, and I heard that people were there in the camp, and that was the first time in my life that I saw, what a camp looked like, that people were simply imprisoned there, that they were fenced off with wire. And we stopped there for a while, and then we continued our journey again or still towards Banja Luka. And then somewhere near Kozarac, I also saw another checkpoint. And a guard came on to the bus who shouted at us in a sense, did we go off to be photographed, that we should have our heads bent as far as we could. And after that, we continued, and I saw that we were going in the direction of Omarska for a moment because I saw the transport line because the transport line was used for mining ore. And this transport line road was going alongside the road itself, parallel with the road. And there were these facilities where people were being kept. And in Omarska, we sat on the bus. We didn't leave. A soldier came on to the bus and asked a person with the last name of Kadiric, let me just think, I can't remember the first name. I believe that his nickname was Muno. Yes, Munib, that was his first name. Munib Kadiric was asked for by this person, but there was no such person on our bus. And we left Omarska, possibly because or probably because there was no room for us. So we used this old road -- that's what we got from the conversation, that we were using this old road.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go from Omarska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I suppose we took the old road because it was no asphalt road. It was a dirt track really. What they used to refer to as the old road through Petrov Gaj. That's where the road led all the way to Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you then arrive in the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We got off the bus, and there was a school building there, a gym, and some sort of a centre, a dome. There was some sort of a department store there, too. It was abandoned. Only the walls standing. And that was that. There was nothing else there. That's where we stayed. A window had been smashed on that shop. It was not very high, so we had to climb on through that window into the building, and then lie down on the tiles, on the floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that at the collection point near the cafe bar in Biscani, that your group was divided in two. Do you know what happened with the other half of the group that didn't go on the bus with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The other group, the other bus, arrived later, after we did. We were on the first bus, but a while later, the other bus came, too. And those people who were ahead of me -- however, when I saw those people, I saw that -- I realised that a number of people were missing in the group, those people who were standing in my close proximity, next to me, those people were no longer on the bus. Later we found out, the same night, because the two groups were mixed and put in the same place, so we started talking to the people from the other group. And they told us their version of the events on the way to Prijedor, they said in Prijedor Skoplje, the bus was pulled over. The person who had singled me out from the line back there who was wearing a helmet was providing security for the bus, but then that person said that people should get off through the back door, and then he simply shot them. That house there, right next to it, that person's nickname was Granata, meaning shell. I can't remember his first or last name, but that's what they called him. There were pits dug next to the house. There were pebbles lying, and the pits were open. We used to call those pits sand pits, and that's where he had the people lined up, and then he shot them. And then the bus continued, they said, directly on towards Trnopolje, and they claimed they stopped at no other places along the way. However, when the bus got to Trnopolje, those people were lined up in front of the bus, and then the same person with the helmet, I had already given you the description, that person that singled out again 12 or possibly 13 people and sent them back to the bus and then on to the village because there were other people waiting in the village and there were other collection points there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before you go on to talk about what happened once the second bus arrived at Trnopolje, I want to ask you a few more questions about what learned had happened at this house owned by the man with the nickname Granata. You said that you noticed some men that you knew from Biscani who had been in the line with you at the cafe bar were missing. Do you remember now any of the names of those people who were at the cafe bar and didn't arrive on the second bus when it got to Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, those were my neighbours, friends, and relatives, all of them. I know their names. Should I give you their names?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The person I've already mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Session if the witness discusses the names of the neighbours?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't think it's necessary because he has already indicated his village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The person I've mentioned before who had been killed next to the cafe bar, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: May I stop you there. May the statement the witness just made about his relationship be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I was afraid of this. And please redact the names in line 16 and 17. And twice in 17.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, Witness X, without telling us how you know these people, just give us the names of the other people that you know were on the second bus and didn't reach Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes. I've given you three names. There were also Nurija Kekic, Halid Kekic, Sabahudin Kekic, Asmir Kekic, Muhamed Tedic, Ferid Risvanovic. I think those people had been taken off the bus when the bus was stopped along the road between Biscani and Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know someone named Vojnikovic, Elvir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, I forgot about him. Yes, he was there, too. Elvir Vojnikovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you were telling us about what happened when the -- after the second bus arrived at Trnopolje. Can you please continue and tell us what occurred to the people on the second bus? You said that some of them were asked to remain on the bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I already said that once the other bus got there, those who had survived were lined up outside the bus and in front of the shop in which we were staying. The front of that building was all glassed over, but glass had been shattered on some of the windows so you could see what was happening outside to a great extent. There were soldiers outside the house, but inside there were no soldiers. So we could see a lot of what was happening in front of the building. Then the person called out the names of 12 people and sent them back to the bus. And then the bus left. We had no idea where it went or where they took those people. But several days later when they had done the things with the men, Serb soldiers began carrying out ethnic cleansing with the women and children up there in the Brdo area and bringing them to the Trnopolje camp. So the families began to be reunited in the camp. So one of the families told us about the events because they walked for a portion of that road, and then the parts of the road I told you about and those locations, that's where they found all the dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The bodies of the men that had been ordered back on the second bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes. The execution site where those people had been killed was a bit further on closer to Prijedor down that road because there is a big bend in that road, a 90 degree bend. And that area is called Kratalj. There was some sort of a pit there. And whenever the River Sana overflows, water collects there, so that plot of land was not good for harvesting because there would always be water there whenever the Sana River overflowed. So that was a very peculiar piece of work. Those 12 people were shot in that place. I had the opportunity to talk personally to one of the survivors there in that place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many people survived among those that were ordered back on the bus, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Two persons survived in the first case. One remained alive and went back to the village and stayed in the village and could not break through because when the military came later on and expelled everyone in an ethnic cleansing operation, they combed the woods, and it was not possible to get out. So he disappeared somewhere in the village. I heard an account by his wife who told me about how he came at night to bring food, and then he would go back to the forest, but then at one point he disappeared, and nothing was later heard of him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: His name was Fikret Sabanovic. And the person who survived and who is still alive is called Nenad Kekic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you speak to Nenad Kekic about what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you get a chance to speak to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: In Germany, that's where I met him, because he spent some time in Germany after the war, the first period following the war. He was in Germany, and then after a while he left Germany.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us what he told you about what happened to the men on the second bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: He told me how they were lying on the floor in the bus, and that they were then returned to Biscani, and then along that portion of the road, the bus was pulled over. They were made to get off the bus, and they were lined up. And then he said somehow he managed to fall down on the ground before everyone else, and then the corpses just piled up on top of him and that saved his life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he say how the others were killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: He said that they were simply machine-gunned. They were shot. It was some sort of an automatic rifle, but it had some sort of a trigger in front. And the bar -- and the barrel was a bit longer, but it was the same type of rifle, the so-called Crvena Zastava, the "red flag" automatic rifle. I was also familiar with that kind of weapon, because when I was in the army, I had that type of weapon myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These men that were ordered to get on the second bus in Trnopolje and most later were killed, did you see any criteria? Did they have anything in common that in your mind could have led them to be selected for execution?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: No, there was no selection criterion, they were people like anyone else, just average people. One of them was a driver who used to work in the company before the war. And one of his workmates who was also a driver and who was wearing a uniform put him on the bus. And all the others were just selected randomly, I'd say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You arrived at the Trnopolje camp on the 20th of July, 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: On the 24th of July. No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 20th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, the 20th of July, that's when I arrived in Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you stayed there until the 21st of August. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges about the conditions that you lived in -- under at the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: As I've mentioned before, there was an elementary school building in the camp, and inside that building there was a gym and a building we called the dom, plus the shop I was talking about. When we arrived in the camp, the next morning, the Serbian Red Cross had us all registered, all the people who arrived on that day and who had spent the night inside the shop. And then we were allowed to join the other inmates. People from Prijedor, Kozarac, and those surrounding villages who had already spent quite a bit of time in the camp. And then we were simply recorded by the Red Cross. And when they registered us, I saw there Slobodan Kuruzovic, who was standing next to the other two persons, two women, with Red Cross insignia, who were recording our names in their books. And I saw Slobodan Kuruzovic standing there. He was a major by rank. Slobodan Kuruzovic had been a teacher of mine in elementary school. He was a teacher of maths at the Mladen Stojanovic elementary school in Prijedor for some time. Outside of school I would often meet him at the Sana River because he was often fishing there, and we sat next to each other quite often near the bridge over the River Sana fishing together. There was a railway bridge, because there was a track leading to Ljubija. And we spent quite some time on that bridge fishing together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Slobodan Kuruzovic say something to you at the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Not on that day, nothing special.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On another day, did he say something to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: After several days there, just outside the school building, inside the camp, we met. He asked me: "Did we really need this? We'll never go fishing together again." He said something like that, as though it had been my fault to have been brought there in the first place. I wanted no debate with him, however, because it was all as clear as day to me, all the horrible things that I had been through up to that point, seeing the camp, being captured and brought to another camp again. I really didn't want to comment. And that's what it was like, but he was there every day in the camp. And every time new convoys of buses arrived taking women and children away, I'd see him there. He had a house inside Trnopolje, and he lived there. I'm not sure if it was the headquarters, but it was some sort of a crucial place in the camp because I know what it means to be a high-ranking officer. That means the highest responsibility. And in those days, at least as far as I could tell, he was the only major in the camp, and all the other officers there were lower-ranking officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court the conditions that you lived under, how you slept, what you ate, in the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The day we got into the camp and to the school building, we didn't really have any proper accommodation. We just walked around. There was no place for us to be put up. Too many people sleeping in the gym, in the school building, in the corridors, and we just slept outside. So whenever we crossed paths with people we knew who had been there for a while, if only we had managed to get a piece of bread until we started to find our way around a bit better. People from the surrounding villages were allowed to leave the camp, leave their ID at one of the checkpoints and go to houses in the surrounding villages to get some food, some vegetables, that people had grown in the surrounding villages, food like tomatoes, because there was a lot of ovens there, cookers, which people then used to prepare food. Those were also cookers from the surrounding houses. It's also important to mention that in Trnopolje, you could buy bread every day but you needed to have money in order to buy bread there. And there was -- Serbian bank notes were being used at that time, and when my mother and sister came to the camp they brought some money with them and gave us that money because they had nowhere else to spend it there in the Travnik area because a different currency was in use over there. So when the convoys arrived whoever knew anyone else in the camp, they just leave them all the money because the money couldn't be used anywhere else. And that was also how we managed to survive. We would order the bread for the next day, and then we would buy it and get it the next day. That was only for a short while, but it was enough, and there was a need to go somewhere. My father and myself always talked about how we should try and join a convoy with the women and children so we could get out, but every time we tried, we failed. Whenever buses and lorries arrived, there would be so many armed people there controlling, checking, in order to keep all the men from getting away and joining the groups of women and children. So for a month, we lived under those circumstances in the camp. Conditions were dreadful. We couldn't wash. There was some sort of improvised toilets, and it was dreadful. It was extremely hot. There were so many flies. I remember clearly things scattered all over the place, garbage. It was -- an epidemic might have broken out at any point.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived, when the people in the camp, were they men, women, were they mixed? And did that change at all in the month that you stayed there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The day we arrived, they were mixed because every two or three days, new convoys of buses and lorries came, and they would only take away women and children. It was like that several times until only men remained. And then I remember clearly it was around the 5th of August when the people had been captured came to Trnopolje on the 6th or 7th August when Omarska was closed down and we were all collected in Trnopolje, we were all staying there at that point, there were only men left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I could break now or I could go on about another 10 or 15 minutes to finish Trnopolje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think it's appropriate to have a break now. The trial stays adjourned until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. And please, proceed immediately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness X, you told us that when you arrived that first night, you couldn't find a place to sleep inside the Trnopolje camp, and you slept outside. Did you later find accommodations indoors, or where did you sleep for the month that you were at the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: All the time period when the convoys were leaving Trnopolje, taking women and children, I didn't sleep indoors. I slept outside. But when the last convoy with women and children left towards Travnik, only men were left, and there were no women and children left, and I managed to find my father and I, we managed to find a place where we would be sleeping together in a sports hall near each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived at the camp, were you allowed to bring anything with you from your home in Biscani?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Nothing, nothing was allowed to be brought along because of the soldiers of Serb nationality. We were searched in going towards the gathering point. We had to empty our pockets of our valuables. They asked for ID cards and so on. But I didn't carry an ID card with me that day, and so I had nothing to give. The only thing I had was what I had on me, the clothes I wore.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were people's families allowed to bring them clothing and food and other necessities, soap?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: My sister managed to bring me a pair of trousers and a jacket when she left the house, and she gave it to me, and I kept it under a blanket where I slept in the sports hall, in a plastic bag. And on that day, on the 21st of August, we set off with the convoy, I put on the trousers and the jacket.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on that -- we'll get to that day. But just this one question: On that day, then, did you wear, then, two pairs of trousers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: You mean on that day, you mean on the 21st of August?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: No, I did not. I only wore one pair of trousers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the conditions at the camp change in any way towards the middle of August, after Omarska was closed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: In no particular way. I just remembered that many delegations came, foreign delegations came. They were moving about inside the perimeter of the camp. Some people were giving statements. In that sense, there was a change.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a sign put up at the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: They would just put up a sign if a delegation was to come, then they would put the sign up. But then they would even take away the wire as soon as an international delegation organisation would come, then they would make it look as if it was a collection or gathering centre of Trnopolje, not a camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recall what the sign said that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I can't remember at this very moment, but it was something like that a collection point or a collection centre, something like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see someone in the camp that you knew named Mirsad Medic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: This person I met during the ethnic cleansing on 20th of July. I met him again on the very first night in the camp. He was the one who was supposed to guard us who were imprisoned in the shop. This was the person with the nickname of Zolka who was working on the Energo petrol station in Prijedor. It was on the Banja Luka Road that the petrol station was located, on the road leading towards Banja Luka. I also remember when the night approached when this same man called Zolka, when he put his head through the door or through the window and asked the people if they needed anything, one man said -- he spoke to Zolka and said he was cold, that he needed a coat, that he was very, very cold, that he was freezing cold. And the two of them, they already knew each other. So perhaps it was for this reason that this person addressed Zolka hoping that Zolka would help him. Because this Mirsad Medic who had been killed at the checkpoint used to be a colleague of Zolka. They used to work together at the petrol station. And so this man called Zolka asked this person who had spoken, the person called Sulejman Kekic how he would he was, and Sulejman Kekic said that he was 70. And then Zolka said to Sulejman, you're ready to be killed or you're mature enough to be killed, and so he him out of the shop and then he beat him in front of the shop. When Sulejman returned into the shop, the only thing that could be heard was his sobbing, his crying. He was sobbing from all the kicks and hits that he received, and nobody said anything. We were all silent because we were not allowed to speak to each other. And then this man called Zolka told another guard to come and wake him up at 2.00 a.m., that he would come and get Sulejman and kill him, and that's exactly what happened. At 2.00 a.m., Zolka came and called out Sulejman, and took him out. Two shots were heard, and Sulejman did not return.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Sulejman Kekic, the man who was killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him. He was a neighbour of mine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just to be clear, Zolka, the person you called Zolka, do you know if he was a member of the police or the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: He was not a member of the police. He was either a member of the army or he was a paramilitary. If I say a member of the army, I know what army was. It is when a person is serving a military service at a certain age when he's after 18 years of age, after finishing secondary school. But all the people who were over 30, 35, 40 years old, these were people who were members of the reserve forces of the army, and they were then mobilised into soldiers, combatants or paramilitary soldiers, what you wish. And he was certainly of Serb nationality, all of them were. And they were all in uniform. And they were all members of paramilitary forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the Trnopolje camp, did you ever hear of a police unit called the intervention squad from Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: We heard what was called Sarenci, that's what it was called. Every time a convoy came to the Trnopolje, this intervention platoon would come, and all the men and myself included were all afraid of these men because these were terrible. We were all afraid of these so-called Sarenci who were actually persons wearing camouflage uniform. And all of these people were frightened of joining the women and children, perhaps boarding one of the buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anything about the uniforms of the men in this unit that distinguished them from the regular police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: This uniform was a camouflage uniform that was worn by the police. It was a police war uniform. It was blue and yellow camouflage uniform with insignia which had a Serbian flag on one side, and on the other side it said "Militia" which means police and that was written in Cyrillic script.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What would happen when members of this unit would show up at the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: As I said already, simply through the experience of the people who had been in there for a -- longer than we had, we all realised that these people were dangerous, that what they did was dangerous. They were very aggressive because, for instance, when the convoy would be loading, then they would appear, and they were there protecting the convoy, guarding it while people were boarding it, boarding the buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they have a vehicle that you recognised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: They had one vehicle, a Ford vehicle, which was a van, and it had a large tiger depicted on it, a large picture of a tiger on that van. It was a white Ford van.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you seen that vehicle or people in those blue camouflage uniforms during the cleansing of Biscani on the 20th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: No, I did not see this vehicle, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were at the Trnopolje camp, did you ever see any representatives of the International Red Cross come to the camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I saw some delegations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you're not sure who they were exactly; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: No, I did not dare because before they appeared, the people who guarded us threatened us that we shouldn't give any statements for our own protection. So we could only see them from a distance. When the delegations were going round visiting looking at the living conditions in the camp, we would be watching them from a distance. We would be sheltering a little, and praying to God that nobody would ask us any questions or interview us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to the convoy on the 21st of August, do you know if the International Red Cross had registered you or other prisoners at the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Before the 21st of August, nobody had registered us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you receive any information as to when the International Red Cross was to begin or began registering inmates at the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Nothing specific, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you later learn that the International Red Cross had come to the camp in August to register the inmates?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, I learned it later because after I left the Trnopolje camp, there were people who were left whom I knew, people who I met four or five months later in December that year. And then they told me that the ICRC came on Monday, the 26th of August, and that they then registered the prisoners -- oh, no. Sorry. 21st was the Friday, 22nd Saturday, so that would have been 24th of August, it would have been Monday. And the ICRC came and registered all the inmates at the Trnopolje camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the time that you left Biscani on the 20th of July up to the 21st of August, did you have much contact with your father?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Father was always near me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 21st of August, what happened that day while you were at the Trnopolje camp?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: On the 21st of August, buses started coming, and only men were boarding them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there women and children left in the camp at that time, the 21st of August?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: That day, there were no women and children left in the camp. There were only men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among the men that were at the camp, were there people who had been released in August from Omarska and Keraterm?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, there were people who were in Keraterm. There were people who had been in Omarska. We were all gathered in Trnopolje, yes, that's correct. There were people from other camps, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the buses arrived, were you told anything by the guards and authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The guards said that we should board the buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the camp commander present when the buses arrived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, he was always in the immediate vicinity, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say or we say the camp commander, who did you understand at that time to be the camp commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I presume that this person was Slobodan Kuruzovic, who was a major, and that he was camp commander or whatever, that he was the main person in the camp, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when -- were the buses loaded in the camp? Can you tell us what happened and particularly what happened with you and your father during that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: At that time, when the buses arrived, this van also appeared, the van that I mentioned earlier. This intervention platoon arrived, so-called. And the bus would come at a time, and then bus would arrive. It would be loaded, and it would leave Trnopolje and go in the direction of Kozarac and a second, third, fourth, and so on. So this is how people were boarding buses. There were no -- not all four buses did not come at the same time. But one bus would arrive, would be loaded, would leave, the guard would board the bus, the prisoners would board, and then he would leave, and then second and so on. On that day, again, I met Dragan Knezevic and managed to have a direct contact with him again. He was wearing this blue camouflage uniform and had an automatic rifle. He had some additional ammunition frames around and some other men also were walking around in this fashion. So it could be noted that -- remarked that they were additionally armed or had additional ammunition. So Dragan addressed me, asked me where I was, that he had been looking for me ever since the cleansing took place, that he couldn't find me in Trnopolje, Keraterm, or Omarska. He said that he was going to save me, that that was his intention, that he would get me transferred to Croatia via Orahova, that was the place near Gradiska, near Sava River, that he would transfer me. That was where UNPROFOR was located. He spoke in this sense. Then he told me to look for my father, that he would help me as well as the other members of my family and people I knew, that he would help us to get on to one of the buses because there was a lot of chaos there. There were a large number of people, and when people went for the buses, there was simply -- things were going out of control, and there was even some firing into the air. In order to stop the people who were going for the buses. Because these people had nothing else left but to go for the buses because they couldn't go back home because everything had been burned or looted. At the time when we were in Trnopolje, it was obvious that all of these -- all the smoke that we could see, this is our houses that had been set on fire and burned down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By the way, did you ever learn what happened to your house?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: As far as our house is concerned, I later found out in 1999. I visited the house, I went to see the house, I was in front of the house. But until then, I only heard stories from other people what actually was happening in the area, that all our property had been looted and that all the houses had been set on fire, mined, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you saw your house in 1999, can you describe the condition and whether you saw any evidence of fire, previous fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: It's like this: The house was derelict. There were no doors. There were no windows. It had all been taken out. There was no roof on the house. And what we called the base of the roof, all that was thrown to the floor, all this had been broken. And so what I did was that I just walked through this destruction, and I went to the house. I saw that the walls were black, that paint had fallen off, and all the traces that told me that the house had been set on fire, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back to the 21st of August, do you remember what the weather was like that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: It was very hot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to get on the first few buses that arrived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, I was, but because Dragan Knezevic insisted I didn't, I did not actually get on the bus. He said that he had no more time to spend with me, and that he had to go to another bus where he was providing security. Then a third bus showed up, and near the bus there was Kuruzovic, Dragan Kuruzovic standing there. He used to know my father. They were together in the Yugoslav army. He told me to go get my father and to get on the bus together, and that's what happened. My father and I, we got on to the bus together. And when the bus filled up with people, it left Trnopolje and continued on to Kozarac. On the road near Kozarac, near the petrol station and the sawmill, we stood and waited. No one informed us why we had to wait, but after a while, lorries showed up from the direction of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the transcript, it indicates that you said that "it was Kuruzovic Dragan" that told you to get your father and get on the bus. What was Kuruzovic's first name?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Slobodan Kuruzovic. Dragan Knezevic was the other person who was with me at the academy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know, on the bus that you and your father boarded, how many people do you think were on that bus? Were there as many people as there were seats?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: You see, those buses were a bit special. They were for urban transportation, and there were more standing places than seats. So you could fit a lot of people inside those buses because the seats were not taking up much space. There was more space to stand than to sit. The bus was full.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you and your bus and the others went to Kozarac, you said you stopped and waited there. And what happened at that juncture of the road at Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: That stretch of the road, as I've said before, lorries and buses Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 6888 to 6895. showed up from the direction of Prijedor. As far as I know, that convoy had been loaded in Tukovi on that same day, the 21st of August, with the same destination, Travnik, or perhaps the separation line, the line of separation near Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After waiting at that point, do you know how many different buses or other vehicles arrived from the group that you believe was loaded in Tukovi? How large was a convoy once everyone was together, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: As far as I could tell, there were four other buses that arrived, plus those four that we were in which had set out from Trnopolje, and then I could also see eight lorries. Some had trailers, and as far as I could tell, there were eight buses and eight lorries. The security was provided by a vehicle manned by some mechanics with a TAM truck, the so-called TAM truck in case the bus broke down, they were there to help and repair it because we had a long way to go. I can't tell you the distance exactly, but there must be about several hundred kilometres between Prijedor and Travnik. And it's a very hilly road. It's mostly hillside. So experience showed that one such vehicle was needed, and that the mechanics, too, had to be there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to the schlepers [as interpreted] or lorries and the buses and the repair vehicle, were there other police vehicles or any other police vehicle escorting the convoy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, there were a number of police vehicles, Golf police vehicles. They led the convoy probably.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the route that you took after the convoy joined up at the Kozarac crossroads?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The road for Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you went through or around Banja Luka, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: We went towards Skender Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have a map entitled "Trnopolje-Vlasic route." It has the ERN number 02166228. May that be given the next exhibit number. And I have copies to distribute to all parties. JUDGE SCHOMBURG: It should be then provisionally S245.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That map is now being placed on the monitor. Witness X, if you could look at it. Does this map depict the blue line -- the line with blue arrows depict the approximate route of the convoy that you were on on the 21st of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that you passed through the road -- more or less through the outskirts of Banja Luka? You didn't go through the centre of town; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you told what -- what was the object, the destination, that you were told that the convoy was going to? Where were they supposed to take you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: We were supposed to reach the line of separation, to simply go there and cross over into territory controlled by Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you know at that time, on the 21st of August, was Travnik controlled by the government in Sarajevo, the non-Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you left Kozarac, were there other stops on the way? Can you please tell us about the stops that occurred.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I remember clearly when the guard on our bus spoke to me and called me by my last name. He ordered me to collect all bank notes from the men on that bus and all their valuables, all the valuables that those men had on them. Their watches, any gold, jewellery they were wearing. I did this, but those people would not give anything away, or perhaps they had nothing on them. But I recall only having collected several bank notes, and that's what I handed over to him. But then he sent me back to the bus. How that person knew my last name -- well, I suppose Dragan Knezevic had already found out everything about my whereabouts and which bus I was on because this security person, I had never met that person before and probably he had not met me either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: May I ask the usher to move the ELMO out of my line of sight with the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After this stop, did you have other stops? What was the next stop stop that you recall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I recall another stop. We waited for a while, and I also remember that the person securing our bus, the guard on our bus, asked me about Edin Mrkalj, whether I knew the person. He used to be a policeman, a member of the police forces. I said I did know the person.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he say? A (redacted) . I can't remember what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, on page 44, line 8, can the first sentence be redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. For evident reasons, the first sentence,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
