utterances.text: Did you know at that time what had happened to Edin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I didn't know, but before the cleansing began, Edin went to the Prijedor Police Station of his own initiative and returned the uniform that he had signed for as well as the weapons. But then he did not return afterwards. He ended up in a camp.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this guard that asked you about Edin tell you what happened to Edin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: No, he didn't. But I already knew at that point what had happened to him, even before this guard spoke to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At one point, did you stop in a wooded area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, the stretch of the road from Skender Vakuf, I remember that at one point, we turned and drove down a dirt track. And then the convoy took -- the convoy was actually so long that vehicles were no longer following one another, but there were larger intervals between them. The ground was very difficult to travel, and it was a dirt track, and the buses and lorries were full. So probably the vehicles had difficulty climbing up the hill. So it was not a very tight convoy, but rather there were quite spacious intervals between the individual vehicles.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you stop somewhere after Skender Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I remember a stop in Skender Vakuf when soldiers got on to the bus, local soldiers from the area in olive drab. They got on to the bus, and they joined us for the rest of the journey.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where did you go then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The same place we were headed before, but I remember that after that, we were pulled over once. We were descending down one side, and there was a creek there. And we were stopped there. And this was the longest stop. And as the buses and lorries were arriving, they were just being lined up one behind the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell us what happened at the stop by the creek.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: We were told to exit the buses, all of us, and to drink water from the creek because we would stop there for a while, they said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see what the policemen were doing at that time while you were by the creek?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I did. They were all together forming a large group, and they were talking about something.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These policemen that were escorting the convoy, did you know if they were policemen from the Prijedor opstina?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes. Only from Prijedor Municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When the policemen in a group talking, after you saw that happen, what occurred?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: We were ordered to line up two by two as though we were going to an exchange.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "we were ordered to line up," was it the prisoners from Trnopolje or were there also people from the trucks and buses that had joined you from Tukovi?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Only people from Trnopolje because those two buses that had set out from Trnopolje were empty, those buses were left empty. And they gathered some more people down the convoy, and they collected more people just randomly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when you were lined up there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: We were lined up and told to get back on to the buses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many buses were you ordered to get into?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I was among the first to get on to the bus, the first bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many other buses were there that the people who were lined up were ordered to get into?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: As far as I could tell, there was just another bus behind us. And the rest, the lorries and the buses, stayed there, and all the refugees, if that's what I should call those people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you got on the first bus. Where was your father?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: He was near me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old were you on the 21st of August?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How old was your father?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: He was born in 1942. He later turned 50 in November, so at that point he was 49.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got on to this bus after the separation at the creek, where the men were separated, how crowded was that bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: We got on through the back door of the bus and headed down towards the front of the bus, and we were then ordered to lie down on the floor. I felt a weight on my back, and those -- that was actually the weight of people lying on top of me. Everything I saw happening at that point, I was trying to see what was happening in front of me because I couldn't turn my head left or right or look behind me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any estimate of how many men were packed on to the bus that you were on at that point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: According to my estimate, roughly a hundred people. I know that when we were being transported from Biscani to Trnopolje, when we headed down the road for Banja Luka when conditions were more normal, at that point, I was able to have a look and see how many people there were on the bus before we got piled up one on top of the other. And when we were allegedly being taken for an exchange, I saw that more and more people started boarding the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were being ordered on to the bus, who was ordering the prisoners to get on to that bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I still remember clearly is this one person in uniform, in police uniform. You could only hear this person's voice. It seems that he was the commander at that moment because his was the only voice heard. This person was armed with a scorpio and a pistol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you later describe, discuss this person's description with your uncle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Later when I met my uncle several years later, when I told him about my version of the events, he told me that that person may have been Dragan Mrdja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe this person that was giving the orders whose voice you heard.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I remember that he had rather thick eyebrows, hair brushed to one side, black hair.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his complexion like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his complexion, his colouring?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: A bit dark.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said he carried a pistol. Can you describe the pistol.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: He was talking about a CZ-99 all the time. He just kept shouting and repeating that word.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that a semi-automatic pistol?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I think it's an automatic pistol actually, CZ probably standing for Crvena Zastava, the red flag, because they made the gun, they produced the gun, the pistol. It must have been something like that, the CZ thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the men in the line were ordered on to these two buses, what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: When our bus was filled, we moved on, and that same person was on our bus, alongside with a handful of other policemen. This person then produced a plastic bag and said to put all our valuables in it. And then the plastic bag was passed down the bus, and then eventually returned to him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far did the bus travel or how many minutes, to the best of your recollection, before it stopped again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I think between 10 and 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened when the bus stopped?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: When the bus stopped, we all had to exit through the front door. And then outside the front door of the bus, there was a group of police officers who were directing us to go back in a column two by two. And then to the right, of course, there was the door of the bus, and then we walked down the road on which we had arrived there walking in a column two by two. My father was walking next to me. I just looked in front of me, because I was not supposed to look left or right. And then I saw a gorge there. We were walking towards a gorge, and it began dawning on me that they would shoot us there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the point where the bus stopped, can you describe the road? Was it a wide road, and what was to the two sides?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: As much as I could see, on the right-hand side, as we returned to the road, there were rocks, rocks just by the road. And on the left-hand side, I remembered some concrete pillars which were like a border post. I just remember those concrete pillars that were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you're talking about the right-hand side as you returned, that is after you got out of the bus, you walked back in the opposite direction that the bus had travelled. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, so the bus was turned in this direction, and we were going back. So on the right-hand side, there were rocks, and on the left-hand side was the abyss, the gorge, and these concrete pillars which I remembered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you described that on the right-hand side there were rocks, are these rocks that you can walk across? Can you describe what was the shape of the terrain at that point? Was it something you could easily cross or was it difficult?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Well, it was like this: On the right-hand side, there were these rocks, and there were going just by the road. And you could see some trees and the wood, and you couldn't walk there. The left-hand side, you could see the abyss because you couldn't see anything there. It was just further there, which I could see the rocks from the canyon. It was almost as if it was a huge gorge, a huge ditch between the road and this other hill. But the further we were going -- closer we were going to this pit, it was more obvious that it was an abyss.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So walking back on the left-hand side was the abyss. On the right-hand side the rocks that you talked about, was that a sheer face of rock that could not be climbed? Just a vertical rock cliff?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, yes, in that sense, they were just like that. Yes, there were just steep rocks, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As the column of men walked back, about how many metres do you think you walked back after getting out of the bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: We walked for about a hundred metres or so. I think I was perhaps fifth or sixth from the start of the column, of the line, and we were walking until we were ordered to stop. And I presumed the people who were at the end of the line, until they saw the abyss, that's when we were stopped because it was all under military command. We were told to walk in two by two, and then the very same person gave orders and said that the line should stop. We did stop. Turn left. We all turned left. Step three steps forward. We did. And then they told us to kneel down. When we kneeled down, then we could see this enormous abyss below us. And here I could hear the person saying: "Here we exchange dead for the dead and living for the living."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which person said that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The same person that I believe is called Dragan Mrdja.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that when you were walking, you were about fifth or sixth from the front in line. When the group of people from your bus lined up, could you see the rest of the group mainly to your left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: No, just as much as I could see -- as much as was in my field of vision.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How close to the cliff, to the abyss, did you stop?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The very edge, on the very edge of the road, very edge of the abyss, if it touched us, we would be down in the abyss. We were on the very edge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was your father?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: On -- standing to my left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: When this person said that he was exchanging dead for the dead and living for the living, that's when the shooting started from firearms. Shooting first came from my right-hand side. I saw that people were starting falling down into the abyss. And I somehow managed to shout at my father, to say to my father: "Father, throw yourself."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to you, then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: He pushed me into the abyss down there, into the precipice.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how far that drop was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: No, I am not clear about that even today. From the very moment when my father pushed me, I do not recall when was it the first time that I actually touched ground. I only felt a couple of times that through the speed, I was turning, and that I was trying to stop. There were some rocks and there was some grass, and a couple of times I realised that I was still alive. But the actual fall on the ground, I do not remember that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your next memory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I remember when I found myself in a sitting position deep down away from the road. And I remember the shooting. That's what I remember most. So I just found myself in that position, and I remember also the time when we were going in the line, left the buses, I had a jacket on me. This jacket was lost. It's almost as if someone had taken it off me. The jacket had flown off me, fallen off me. I had no sport shoes on my feet. When I woke up, I had no sports shoes. I was all bruised all over my body. But the worst injury that I had was that I had broken my ankle of my right foot. I don't know how even my foot was just hanging on by some kind of a -- some tendon. It was the pain that actually woke me up, and I was apalled at what I saw as being my injury. And shortly afterwards, I also remember that moment when I saw two men who had come down to the abyss and were going round and shooting at people in the head, and I just waited for them to come and shoot me. Then I could see them, that they turned back. They were going sideways in order to get back to the road. Nobody did anything to me. I just remained sitting down. In fact, I had -- by that time, I pretended to be dead and I had lied down, although this was -- I was going to tell you, it was a kind of clearing. They would have been able to see me, but I still can't make it clear to myself why I was not killed then. I also remember that that time period while I was sitting there next to me, there were some bags and some things that people had taken with them. It was all thrown into the abyss. And there were also some rocks and stones that were there because there was still the rest of the abyss which goes round down to the small river. So I also heard some shooting which was coming from my left side, and I presume that this was the second bus that what it could have been because I had the opportunity to speak to the survivors from the second bus. So I presume that it was the location in question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What time of day was it when the massacre happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: In the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you recall being awakened by the pain or regaining consciousness and hearing shooting. At that time, where was the shooting? Could you tell where it was coming from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The first few moments I recall because I looked behind me. I looked up towards the road where people were standing. And I thought the firing was coming from there, and perhaps a little bit further on. From my left side, there was some shooting coming, but these were large hits, as if there were some kind of hand-held rocket launchers or something. But this is what I could hear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to be clear, when you talk about what's coming from the road and you say your left side, is that looking from where you were up to the road it would be to the left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, when I say from my left-hand side behind my back, behind me there were people up a hill who had been killed. But when I'm saying "left," I suppose this is another place where these people could have been. So it wasn't quite behind my back. It was a little bit to the front of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were conscious there, did you see the bodies of other people who had been on your bus?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, I saw the bodies. I saw some bodies. But perhaps I survived because I was the one who went the furthest away from all the others because I went the furthest -- deepest into the abyss. So some of the bodies were stopped 10, 15, 20 metres before me, and I saw some of those bodies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you saw two soldiers walk down and you heard pistol shots. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after they left?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: After they left, I already heard the shooting, as I said, coming from my left side. And when this shooting died down, it was then that I saw the convoy, the convoy that had been stopped down there, passed by the road down to the confrontation line. It was in the late hours of the afternoon. And I also saw this convoy when it returned empty using the same road. And to me, this meant that this confrontation line was nearby, and that I thought that although injured, somehow I would manage to get to the confrontation line and save myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to walk?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: No. I was not able to walk because this ankle was broken, and it completely came out of a joint. It was just -- my foot was just hanging. It had no connection to the bones. I had no feeling that I had been shot by a bullet. I presume that this was a sharp rock that had hit me as I was tumbling down.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you do anything to stop the bleeding?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: That day, I did not do anything. I just waited for nightfall so that I would get to some water because my body needed water. I did not dare to go further down because there was shooting all around. And I started to see things wrongly. I started to have hallucinations, so I waited for nightfall, waited for sun to set. And I was trying to get down to the water slowly on my hands, and this is -- I spent my first night there by that water. As I was lying during that time before night, there was a bag that belonged to some person that was near me. And from that bag, I took a -- the top of the track suit because it was cold, so I spent the night by the river drinking the water. And I decided to follow this river, and I could hear the sound of the water running. And my only hope was that I would get to river where it was wider so that I would throw myself in the river and the river would take me somewhere. That's the thought that led me. So I followed this river and I could just hear the sound of the river running. But I didn't go to swim, and the problem was that perhaps there was not enough rain at the time, and the river was quite shallow. So I couldn't throw myself into the river, and I couldn't walk. So I was crawling on all fours, on my knees and on my hands, and this -- I took a belt from my trousers, and I took the T-shirt off, and I took that and managed to somehow bandage my foot. But there were flies starting to gather on me because I was all covered in blood. So somehow I crawled alongside that river on that first day. That's what I remember. And according to what I could gather, this must have been Saturday.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you seen any other survivors up to that point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: That first day following the execution, just before nightfall, I saw one person who was coming towards me, climbing down the rocks because when it is night you could then hear everything. And I could see and hear somebody approaching. He simply did not notice me because it was dark. It was night. But I spoke to him, and he was also trying to get to the river, and then to go somewhere where it was safe.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did this person -- did you know if it was someone who was on your bus and had survived the massacre?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: No, I presumed this person came from behind my back where all these person had stopped falling from that direction.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he try to help you in any way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I think that I addressed him, and I said I had no foot or I had no leg or something like that. And he just carried on down there. He just continued, and so I just gritted my teeth, and I went towards the water. That's all I could do. This water probably saved my life.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far could you crawl in that time? Let's say in an hour, how far would you get?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: That day, on Saturday, somehow, I had some strength, I had more strength. And I followed the river on that day. But I seem to believe that I was seeing things, I seemed to be seeing soldiers who were shooting towards me. I believe I had hallucinations. And then on the other side of the river, and I was going downstream, so I was on its left bank, on the other side, on the right bank, there were also some rocks. And among those rocks, I kept seeing soldiers and rifles pointed towards me. And I was so afraid that I didn't even dare drink water. And even just by the river itself, I would just have to lower my hand into the water and get some water, but I didn't dare even have an idea that I should cross the river diagonally and that I would make it impossible for them to see me and they wouldn't see me then because I would be in their blind spot. And this is what I tried to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You tried to cross the river?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, I tried to cross the river, also on all fours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did it take you to crawl across the river?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I think, as far as I could recall, this was on Sunday only when I managed to cross the river.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after you crossed the river?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Then I also remember the moment when I crossed over to the other side, then there was a storm that started. There was -- rain started. Then I saw an abandoned mill which was roughly the middle of the river. This wasn't a full river. There were lots of small river islands and rocks, and there was this abandoned mill. And I decided again from that other bank to enter the mill because there had been no rain. There was this storm that started because I remember throughout the time I was in the camp rain hadn't fallen. It was on that day that rain started to fall. When I was injured and when the rain started, I hid in this abandoned mill. I remember that this mill was made of wood, and there was no roof. There was just the roof frame. It was an old mill. It was an old mill, old house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the condition of your ankle? You said the first day, some flies were landing on the blood.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I was without any strength, and I tried to get the flies away. I took a little branch with some leaves to get rid of the flies, so I was waving that in order to get rid of the flies because I had been injured. And I had a lot of blood because I had bruises and cuts. And the first day on Saturday, I was waving that with a branch, and then later on I just stopped because I just couldn't do it any more. I was too exhausted. But I know that the T-shirt that I had taken off me which I had put over the foot, it was a black T-shirt, but it was all white from all the eggs that the flies had left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened after you got to the mill?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: This mill, in the meantime, I would be losing it really about day and night differences. I just remember the river bed and the rocks on both sides. I could just see the sky within a hundred metres and that was it. That was all I could see. I had no orientation as to when was day and when was night, and then suddenly I heard some voices. And I saw some people who were in the mill, who had taken the mill. And they spoke to me. And they thought that I had a bomb or something or a grenade on my foot because I had it -- the T-shirt was over my foot because it was pear-shaped. And so then they saw it and they were apalled because they took pity on me of sorts and nobody beat me and nobody mistreated me then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these people you saw in the mill soldiers or civilians?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: These people had olive drab uniforms on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this would be an appropriate time. I'm not sure, is this the lunch break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Trial stays adjourned until 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.57 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Please, proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness X, the location where the executions took place on Vlasic mountain, do you know what that particular place is called, or did you ever learn the name of that place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes. I learned that the name of the place was Koricanske Stijene, and the river that runs there is called Ugar. I learned this from a man from the area who was with me in Banja Luka when I was detained, and he was detained, too. And I had occasion to speak to him several times. I told him my story, and he somehow figured out that that was the place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about meeting one of the survivors, I believe the day of the massacre, later that afternoon. Did you ever see that person again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, I did, the next day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened then when you saw the person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: That person approached me and we talked. I also remember we talked about that, and in my ignorance, I was talking about soldiers who had given me bread nearby there. I was saying something along these lines. And then the person tried to help me. I tried to lean on his shoulder and hop along on one leg so that he could get me out of that place, but we failed. So he left me there, and then I remained alone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say in your ignorance, you talked about soldiers giving you bread, explain what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: At that moment, these were the thoughts I had, those were my impressions at that time. It's as simple as that. Because I did not really see what was happening. I did not see the overall picture. I was living in my own thoughts, in a manner of speaking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you believe that you were having some hallucinations at that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about crossing the river on your own. About how wide was the river at that point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: How wide? Between 20 and 30 metres I guess.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did it take you to cross that 20 or 30 metres?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: A lot of time. I remember when I stopped at about halfway through or two thirds of the way through the width of the river, I remember those moments, but I did take an awful long time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the site or on the convoy or at the actual site of the execution, you said you saw some policemen you recognised from Prijedor. Do you recall the names of those individuals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, I do. At the execution site, I recognised, again, Dragan Knezevic. I also recognised Sasa Zecevic who was also at the academy with us in Sarajevo. I recognised Zoran Babic who was also wearing a uniform with police insignia. Zeljko Predojevic, who was wearing an olive drab uniform. He was an ex-schoolmate of mine from my earlier school days. I recognised Branko Topala who lived in Tukovi, and he was a security guard at the Trnopolje camp at the time when I was in the camp. I also recognised a neighbour, Topala's neighbour -- I think his nickname was Dado, I think he was there, too -- near the bus.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that some soldiers came to the mill and saw your leg. You unwrapped the T-shirt around your leg. After you did that and they saw your foot, what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: After that, they told me not to go anywhere from that water mill. They said they would come there and rescue me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you wait for them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I didn't even budge. I was hoping that they would be back to rescue me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Well, the same persons came back with a horse, and there was some sort of a seat on the horse made of wood, and that's where they put me. They tied me on to the horse's back with rope. I had no power, no energy, to cling on, but that's how they then began to take me away from there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did they take you to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: At first, we started heading back down the river, but the other side, the other river bank, not the one I crawled down. And very soon we went further from the river and started to climb up a hill.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: We climbed some sort of elevation. There was some sort of a checkpoint there. I remember clearly, there were soldiers. And they blindfolded me. They took a bandage, wrapped it around my head so I couldn't see where I was being taken to. I only know that it was a long trek for me and a strenuous one, too. I was seated, and my foot was sort of dangling. The ground was difficult to travel jumping from stone to stone, so to say, because the horse found it difficult to proceed. So I kept dangling and screaming from pain. I kept asking for water all the time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did the soldiers with the horse finally take you to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: That was in the middle of the night, because it was evening when I had been found by those soldiers. So now, I think it was 1.00 past midnight when we reached a village, probably the slopes of the -- of Mount Vlasic. When we reached the village, they lowered me on to a blanket to lie down, and a doctor came along who gave me two injections, one to kill the pain, and one against poison apparently. And then I was taken to -- was it a school building? Some building, at any rate, with beds in it. There was a hall. I don't know what sort of a building it was, but I know that that's where I spent the night until the next morning. And the next morning, a car came along, an all-terrain vehicle, a Lada Niva car. That's what the brand was. They came to take me to Skender Vakuf. I was escorted by the person who had taken me away from that canyon into which I had fallen. So this was the person who saw me, too. Skender Vakuf, the hospital there, and that's where I received first aid. However, soon after, I was sent to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you taken to in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: In Skender Vakuf, I entered the ambulance, the vehicle, and before I left Skender Vakuf, another person got in, a person wearing a uniform, who sat in front of me, and then I gave a statement to that person. This person tape recorded my statement, and I couldn't see the person's face because I was sitting in the ambulance just staring at the ceiling. And this person was seated in the front seat of the vehicle. He told me that he was tape recording my statement, so I should beware and not tell any lies since my statement was being tape recorded. In Skender Vakuf, when I came to the medical station -- when I entered the ambulance and when -- and after I had given the statement, another survivor appeared, and then the two of us went together to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go to in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: At first, as far as I could tell, we went to some sort of headquarters to get a certificate in order to be able to enter -- to be admitted into the medical station, surgery. Once we obtained our permission, we were admitted into that ward, the surgery, in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you got to the Banja Luka hospital, did they clean your wound?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: When I got into the hospital, they began to clean my wounds. They ripped the trousers I was wearing with a pair of scissors. And then they took me by elevator, I think, to the second floor to a room on the second floor. And then another uniformed person came, a colonel, to whom I also gave a statement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you talk about these two statements, do you mean you talked about the massacre that you experienced on Mount Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, only about the massacre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When your wound was cleaned, did you look at your ankle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there anything that you saw in your wound, in your skin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: It was worm infested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Judges about your experience at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: After I had given the statement, I was taken back to surgery. I was anaesthetised there, allegedly in order to be operated on. But when I woke up, my whole leg was in a plaster cast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say your whole leg was in a cast, how high did the plaster go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The whole length of my leg. That's how long it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Then I was taken to Room Number 7. There were two beds in that room, and three other men. I was the fourth. So the two of us shared one of the beds, and the other two men share the other bed. We were subjected to severe beatings there and torture. My wounds were no longer being dressed, and I was not being given any medical assistance. My organism needed water badly, but there was no water to be had. We were made to drink our own urine then. And that's what we did. We were, so to speak, isolated from all the other wounded persons. The hospital was teeming with wounded people, invalids. All of them were curious, and with the permission of the guards who were watching us, all of the invalids were given a chance to beat us in their own way. Many of them were without a leg or without an arm walking on wooden crutches through the hospital. They would come to our room and just beat us everywhere. They would come back from the centre of the town drunk when the hospital officials were no longer around, only the nurses. So they just come back at night, switch off the lights, draw the curtains, and just beat us in every possible way. I suppose the hospital staff must have known about what was happening to us, because we then got evacuated from Room Number 7, and there was another room next to ours, Number 8, with people whom I had met the day when we were transferred to Paprikovac in Banja Luka. That was also sort of hospital on a hill above Banja Luka. Military police officials came there for us with an ambulance, and they took us to ophthalmology and the Pediatric ward because that's where the only beds were. But even there, we were still isolated and watched over by the guards. The transfer itself from one place to the other was also difficult. Everyone was just waiting for us. We were practically running a gauntlet on our way out of the hospital. The other patients were just beating us with no sympathy whatsoever. And our arrival at Paprikovac, we were received there almost the same way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were the other patients that shared Room 7 with you? What was their nationality, if you know or ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: There were Croats there, too, but mostly Muslims. But there were Croats there. I remember a number of Croats there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember a Croat with the name of Damir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Damir, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to Damir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Damir was transferred with us from surgery to Paprikovac. One day, they just took him away, and he never returned. He was beaten most -- the most of all the prisoners because supposedly he had been brought in wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about being beaten by patients, and you said some would come back drunk from the centre of town. Who were these people? Were they patients? Were you beaten by anyone besides other patients at the hospitals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The patients beat us, the police, the military, civilians who probably came there to visit their own kin who had been wounded on the front. That's the sort of people who were beating us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the doctors or medical staff of the hospital ever do anything to protect you during those beatings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: They probably did try. The head of clinic, as far as I knew, I think his name was Kustric, so probably they did try something. But they have their working hours, and this was happening at night. After nightfall, in the dark, and not during their duty and office hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said your leg was put in a cast that went from your foot to your groin area. What happened to your wound during that time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The day we were taken to Paprikovac, there were three beds in the room. And I was lying in the bed next to the window. It was a very hot day. My wounds were festering, and the whole ward was stinking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The ward was stinking because of your wound, because of your leg?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was the cast taken off?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: The cast was taken off the next day. I asked for a transfer, to be transferred -- to be put near the door, the entrance door to the room because there was no sun there. And that's when the cast was taken off. The plaster cast, but then they put on a different kind of cast up to my knee. Prior to that, they had cleaned my leg. But then after they had taken off the cast, I saw an enormous amount of worms all over the cast and my leg. Where my ankle was supposed to be, there was only hollow. And there were cotton pads inside that hole where my ankle was supposed to be. It was only stuffed into the hole. I saw the doctor when he did it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw the doctor put the cotton into the hole in your ankle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I saw it when he took the cotton wool out, and I saw it when he was cleaning this wound.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the cotton must have been put in and the cast put on when you were unconscious because of some anaesthesia at the first hospital. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. Because when the cast was taken off, when it was cut with scissors, that's when I saw the cotton wool and everything that was in the leg it was in the cast, so it was probably done when I was unconscious, when I had been given anaesthesia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know which doctor had put that cast on you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I don't know which doctor had put the cast on when I had been anaesthetised, but I know which doctor had taken the cast off and which doctor had put the splint on after the cast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you remain in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: In Paprikovac, I remained until the 15th of October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: After that, in that time period, while I was still in Paprikovac, until about 15th of October, the same person came to whom I had given the statement when I arrived at the hospital. And this person asked me if I had anything family members in Banja Luka, and Serb authorities would not charge me with anything, that I was free to go.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you then go and stay with someone you knew?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: No, I did not. For that reason, I had relatives and friends. They were also fighting to stay alive, and it was also difficult for them in Banja Luka. And these family members would not have been able to help me because they would have needed to transfer me somewhere else because I was in a difficult situation. So in Banja Luka, there was this Merhamet organisation which helped people, and it was through Merhamet that I went to the mosque. And that's where I was the whole time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long did you stay at the mosque? When did you leave Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: According to my assessment, about 20th of November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the hospital, in Banja Luka, how was your foot finally treated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: When they put the splint on my leg, I was then transferred possibly because of strong sunlight and because of all the wounds that were very odourous, I was then taken to the front of the room, and I was there for a few days. And then a doctor came, and he was escorted by guards. We were in those few rooms in Paprikovac, and we were guarded by guards. And they would let in people who they wanted to let in, because it was all under their control. And every time when a surgeon would have to come in or somebody else, they would do it depending on their own goodwill or not, as the case may be. So that day, a surgeon came in to dress my wounds, and this guard said that I should not be looked at, something like this will be cut off. And then I realised that I will not have the leg for much longer, and that most of it probably will be cut off.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your foot amputated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Above the ankle?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, yes, about 15 centimetres below the knee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like now to show you some photographs. The first photograph --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMIJIAN
utterances.text: I have various sets that should be distributed now before I begin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: First of all, are there any objections to admit S245 into evidence, the map?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: S245 admitted into evidence. May we then proceed with S246-1, -2, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, S246 is a set of 24 photographs. And they all should be in the same order so I can go through and briefly describe them while we all mark our copies. Everyone has their copy, I can begin. Before they are shown to the witness, I'll describe them. S246 is a photograph of a road with the rock face to the right. I believe that's a view looking toward Skender Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: -1. 246-2 would be looking down an abyss or a gorge. 246-3 is looking over the edge of an abyss. 246-4, again, the bottom of the gorge. 246-5 would again be a view of the road with the rock face to your right, apparently looking towards Skender Vakuf. 246-6 is, again, the gorge. 246-7 is the gorge. 246-8 looking down, and there appears to be some kind of tree felled in the right-hand side of the photograph. And it appears to be something man made in the centre, something white. 246-9 is the rock face to the left. It's a photograph of the road looking towards -- I believe Smet or towards Travnik. 246-10 is the bottom of the gorge. 246-111 is a photograph of a UN vehicle and an ICTY investigator on the road. 246-12 is a photograph of a long view of the area, I believe, looking across the gorge towards the other side. 246-13 is a still longer view looking towards the hill on the opposite side of the river. 246-14 is a close-up of one of the concrete pillars on the side of the road, as is 246-15. As is 246-16, even closer view. 246-17 is another pillar. 246-18 showing the area of the river bed, I believe. 246-19, view of the road with the rock face to the right and UN vehicle parked there. 246-20 has the rock face to the left, the UN vehicle visible. 246-21 is the bottom of the gorge. 246-22, again, the bottom of the gorge. 246-23 appears to show a sheer cliff. And 246-24, again, shows the sheer side of the cliff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any objections?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence as S246-1 to S246-24.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I wonder if it's possible to give the witness a set of photographs that are marked so he can pick out the ones, and then we can have the numbers available.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness X, we're first going to show you 246-1, an exhibit. I ask you to look at that, and do you recognise this area at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: No, no, I presume that these are photographs from the location where the execution had taken place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I understand you presume that, but you have not been shown these photographs before. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: No, I have never seen photographs. I find it a little hard. Yes, yes, you can go on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there anything on -- perhaps you can look through the photographs, and just comment if you recognise any of the areas depicted and if you have any comments you want to make.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: May I begin?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: First of all, here, I selected one of the photographs which for me is the most poignant in some way, because in this position where the vehicle is parked, I presume that the execution had taken place here by the rocks in here. This hill here, this is where the bus had stopped. This is the bus where I had been with my father. This is where the bus had stopped. And from this place, we started to walk up this road, as I have explained already.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. And for the record, can we get the number of that photograph from the usher. The photograph the witness was referring to, S246-20. On the video it was a bit difficult to see because of the glare. Can we have that brought back -- put back on the ELMO. And perhaps the ELMO could be moved a little bit to get rid of the glare on the rock. I don't know if you can do anything for that. Okay. So you're saying that the bus that you were in, there's a very large boulder on the right-hand side of the road looking at this photograph. Your bus stopped somewhere around where that boulder is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, this large rock on the right-hand side, on the photograph, this large rock alongside this rock, this is where the bus was stopped here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then you walked back, would it be correct -- where on this photograph, if anywhere, does it show the area where you were ordered to stop and walk to the edge of the cliff?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps a little bit further, a little bit forward.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In other words, in the foreground of the picture, somewhere around the area that whoever took the photograph was standing. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Well, approximately there, perhaps a few more metres forward, according to my estimate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You talked about remembering seeing some posts. Do those posts appear in these photographs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, these posts are remarkable. You can see them. This is where I could see them -- I saw them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you're referring to those concrete -- small concrete pillars right at the edge of the abyss, about --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes, these that you can see one behind the other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you see anywhere in those photographs the area where you fell?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: On this photograph here, although it is the same photograph, but here I can see a kind of a wall. It is possible to see the wall down which I was looking.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: And for the record, that is photograph number 11.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do these photographs appear to be of the site where the execution took place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I presume so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Okay, thank you, Mr. Usher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness X, in the hospital in Banja Luka, did you meet other people who had survived the massacre at Vlasic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Yes. I met people in Paprikovac, that was in Paprikovac in Banja Luka. These people who had survived these executions. As it happened, they were not physically injured like I was. They were mobile. How they survived, in what way, in fact, I couldn't tell you. But it was only occasionally that I spoke to them because their orders as when we had to go to the toilet in a bucket, the orders were for them to gather that because there was one guard and there were three rooms. And sometimes one would be talking, and that's how we managed to speak during the toilet breaks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the site of the massacre, you said that the last thing you recall on the cliff was being pushed from behind. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I said that this was my father.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see your father again, or his body? I'm sorry, the interpreter did not get your answer. Can you say it again, please.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: I never saw my father again, either dead or alive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, have any of the bodies of those that were killed on Vlasic been recovered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: As far as I know, no. The only thing I recall, the bodies, as I was struggling to survive or to stay alive after that crime on the bank of the river, I saw two dead bodies. And these were, so to speak, freshly dead people. They seemed to have been just killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it matter in your culture and to your personally that these bodies have never been recovered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS X
utterances.text: Well, of course it bothers me. Of course, it upsets me. It's my father. I loved him a lot and respected him. And he disappeared. I never saw him again. I think that I would feel better if I could find out one day where his remains are so that I could erect a monument for gratitude simply, in that sense, I mean. I relied on him a great deal, and we had a good relationship.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness X.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I don't have any further questions at this time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I believe it's appropriate to start with the cross-examination only tomorrow morning. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we do..

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any other points to discuss today in the absence of the witness? Please, Witness X, understand, the Defence, of course, has the right also to put questions to you. And we will ask you to answer these questions in the same way, in the same manner, as you did vis-a-vis the questions put by the Office of the Prosecutor. This will take place tomorrow at 10.00. I thank you for today, and you're excused for today. May the usher please escort the Witness X out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May we please take the opportunity of the remaining time to discuss some issues. There was presented a lot of material related to military expertise. I don't know whether the Defence got these documents in time, because admittedly for us, it was a little surprise to see this volume of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence actually, the lawyers, did receive the military analyst's report without the background in which we can examine whether he qualifies necessarily as an expert. But our objection not just to the voluminous nature of the document is that the report itself is not interpreted for our client to review, and for him to assist us in preparing his Defence. I'm not sure if that's forthcoming, but that would be really our only objection to the report at this time. And obviously we would reserve the right to make any objections based on the qualifications of Mr. Brown at the time when we get his complete curriculum vitae.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And I take it that Mr. Brown will appear as a witness here in the courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And what about the translation, will it be provided in due course?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: It has been submitted, and I do not have a date. We'll check on what the due date is from CLSS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. Then we have got one expertise on handwriting. Is this available for you in both languages, also for Dr. Stakic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It is not, Your Honour. We only have it in the English version, and we did not yet have an opportunity to discuss it with Dr. Stakic in detail. But we did reference it in several conferences that we had with him. We do not have it in a language in which he can understand and most certainly don't have the attached article which seems to be the basis which gives us a five-point guideline on how they rate the analysis that was done by the expert. So we do not have either the report or the bases that the expert apparently relied upon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes. As regards the guideline, the same seems to be true as far as I can see. But probably I'm mistaken, on the basis what I could find today on my desk, that the -- in the expertise mentioned guidelines are not attached.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I see. The Defence did not get a copy of the guideline, as you're referring to. It's about a three-page document. I can provide it. But it's simply a standard -- Ms. Karper says it was filed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may, we do have the report, and we also have the four-page article that's attached to the report. We just don't have it in a language in which our client can fully understand or appreciate, although we have discussed it briefly with him. But we don't have also the qualifications of this purported expert, although I understand that he comes from a reputable institute. We still think we should at least be given his background information and -- because the report itself is somewhat ambiguous. It talks about one individual on the first page, then references, who may be the actual content of the report, another individual. So if we could perhaps get some clarity on that, it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would appreciate the Court's guidance on one matter that counsel raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: If the attachment is the one with the head line "Netherlands forensic institute, forensic handwriting analysis," if this is the guideline, then indeed it's in our hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, that is it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay. What about the translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I submitted it when I received the handwriting report last week I submitted the report. I did not submit that background material on the institute. Interpreting the rule that only the report has to be translated, but that's the matter I wanted Your Honours' guidance on. If Your Honour feels it's necessary, we will submit that also for translation. But Your Honour has seen that document. It simply explains how handwriting analysis is done and the significance of the various results.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I would appreciate very much if the Defence counsel could live with this additional attachment, and if necessary, explain it to your client because, indeed, this is a kind of basis on what the expert is working on. So this could be feasible, I believe. Can we agree that this translation is not necessary?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sure we can, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you already make up your mind, what about the cross-examination of this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The Defence has made up their mind, Judge, in part, only - and I say in part because we would like to consult with Dr. Stakic once he has the report in the language in which he can understand. And also, I would like to have the -- and again, not to repeat myself, but the CV or the background information on the two individuals who appear on page 1 of 7 of the report so that we can determine if and whether it's necessary. But quite frankly, looking at what we coin "guidelines" and the report, we think that comparing it to other institutes that do forensic handwriting analysis we believe it would be necessary at least at this time to cross-examine the witness who is providing this report. We would need some guidance also because the way that the report can be subject to some interpretation. I spoke briefly with the OTP on that. I don't want to share the contents of our conversation, because I don't want to misrepresent what they had said. But I think it's necessary, perhaps, for both sides if the Court gives us their view, as to what weight if any they will give this report. Certainly, we would like an opportunity to cross-examine. We're anticipating and are contemplating calling our own forensic handwriting expert to make a similar if not what we believe a more thorough analysis of the materials that were provided, and hope to she what his or her conclusions are at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I think then the best way to proceed already now, because it's always difficult to get some time window for expert witnesses, to try to summon during the remaining time this witness after the first reading, I also have the impression that from the side of the Judges, there will be the one or other question. So therefore, I invite the OTP to try to summon the witness at an appropriate point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I'll do that. The witness is now on holidays, I know, and out of the country. But we'll find out when the witness returns and try to work out a date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. What about the other expertise as regards making use of the same machine, printer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That could only have been done once the handwriting was complete. I spoke to the expert from the same lab, a different expert, who is doing that. The last I heard was that October was the earliest we could expect the results.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So you regard it as Defence material already now? To be serious, I think we have to live with this and probably we can introduce this only later. It will not disturb your possible motion on acquittal. Third point, indeed, is the question, what about the documentation on the interrelationship between the documents we have before us?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Actually, I received before I had to go on a business trip last Thursday I believe a draft copy of a very long, very difficult, detailed, report regarding the linguistics, et cetera. I've skimmed it, but I don't think any of it sunk in last week. I'll try again this week. I'm not sure when that will be in final form. Hopefully soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But please, as soon as possible taking into account the rules governing expertise witnesses. But this would be an in-house witness. Right?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Finally, there are some remaining points, probably they are resolved without our knowledge during court recess. The last time we asked for four pages of Kozarski Vjesnik in a colour print. Everything is well-prepared as I can see by Ms. Karper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I have the Kozarski Vjesnik, Ms. Karper has just handed to me, Exhibit 242-1 through 242-4, ERN numbers 01469741 through 44. I believe that's the 17th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: They were already admitted into evidence. It's only a copy, one copy for the Court and one for the Defence, please. Anything else to be resolved immediately?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We do, Your Honour, unfortunately. In speaking of the Kozarski Vjesnik, we requested to the Court, and we believe the Court instructed or ruled, ordered, the OTP to provide the Defence with copies of the relevant materials with respect to newsletters and items that appeared in Kozarski Vjesnik for the time period of the indictment, April through September of 1992. We have not yet been provided with copies of those materials. In addition to that, we also requested that all the Crisis Staff orders purportedly that were found or during a subpoena or in any other manner that were seized, that they also be produced. We have not received those items as well, Your Honour. And I have two other points, but I think maybe we should take these separately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Step by step. Kozarski Vjesnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: My memory is not the best, but as I recall the Court's ruling, it was that the Kozarski Vjesniks would be available to the Defence to go through at the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I haven't had a request or time suggested. As I indicated, these are -- we don't have multiple sets. They are signed out at various times by different people. So we have to work with the schedule and see what we can provide at various times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So you invite the Defence to go through your archive as regards Kozarski Vjesnik. The same is true as regards the orders of the Crisis Staff, or is there any helping tool to find it in your computer system?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, there was a project that was ongoing when we took the break. I was away for a short time, and I have been on a business trip for the last week. I'll check on, it but I believe we have a list now of all Crisis Staff decisions in-house. And we can give that to the Defence and compare and see if you're missing any. This was also part of the same project, to answer the Court's question about which decisions appeared in the Gazette. So I hope we will have a spreadsheet available. I'll check on it today and see if it will be available tomorrow, I'm not sure whether it's available yet, which will show all the Crisis Staff decisions and whether or not they also appeared published in one of the Gazettes. THE COURT: May I ask, what about number 1 of the Official Gazette, was it found in the premises of the OTP?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: My understanding is that the Official Gazette number 1 would be not the Crisis Staff, that would be the Municipal Assembly of Prijedor headed by president Cehajic. That would be a separate publication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It is not enough for relevance to say it's interesting to see, but I really wonder having seen the dates of number 2 and 3 in the middle of the year whether or not this number 1 was already one of the Official Gazette, and then to see the difference between, if it's your opinion it still was a normal Official Gazette as opposed to the other Official Gazette, that one can really find out the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that his a matter that' really not in my opinion, but Mr. Corin who is our in-house expert on matter, he is a linguist and a historian, he's reviewed those, and I believe as I recall that's his explanation to me. The decisions did not begin to be published until the Serbian Municipality of Prijedor reconvened the Serbian assembly and adopted the Crisis Staff decisions. So the decisions were not published in the Gazette until the decisions of the Crisis Staff were actually taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Finally from my point of view, sorry, is it your intention under some jurisdiction, it is mandatory, even if you know that a witness will make use of the right not to answer any questions, to call Mr. Mrdja, to call Mr. Brdjanin, to call Mr. Talic or others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: It's not our intention, because I actually believe it will be a futile exercise. Actually we haven't discussed it, but you asked if it was our intention, we didn't have that intention to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Only the question of the intention, and we have to find out, you know, of course different legal systems, in some jurisdictions --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Obviously, they could testify if they wanted to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It could cause a reason for appeal if you don't, at least, try, a reason for appeal for both sides. So one has also to take this question into account how to react on this. I think in addition, available would be possible in a broader connection, Mr. Gruban. Is it your -- I understand that it's not your plan to hear any person already in this entire area arrested, indicted, or even convicted even if it's not final, person, to hear one of these persons, to call one of these persons?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: That's correct, we did not have the intention to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Is it the intention of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We don't believe that it will be necessary, Your Honour, to call them. But we would ask that the OTP provide us with the interviews that they have conducted with those defendants as well as other defendants, including the Plavsic Krajisnik defendants who they have extensively interviewed. We think it's their obligation to give us that complete picture. We don't know whether we would utilise it or not because we don't have access to that information. Likewise, if they did take a statement from Mr. Brdjanin or General Talic or Mrdja, we would like that as well so we could make an informed decision once we have had the opportunity to review that material. To date, we don't have that, and the OTP has steadfastly refused to provide us with that what we think is that relevant information under an obligation that should be ongoing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Well, we believe we've complied with our Rule 68 obligation regarding these matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: But you have had some other issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, just to respond to the Court with respect to the Kozarski Vjesnik, would it be permissible, and we would like to know if the OTP would agree to have our investigator from the region come here so he would exercise those newspaper articles. He is approved obviously by the Registrar. Just because of time constraints Mr. Lukic and I are unable to do that, so we would like to at least orally and formally make that request to the Court and to the OTP if they wouldn't mind us having this investigator who has been on staff with us since the beginning of the case from my understanding to come in and examine those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: If I could just get together with counsel with proposed dates informally and then run it by my office and then we see if there's a disagreement to bring to the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Two other points if I may, Your Honour, one was also -- and not to start the week on any critical note, but we were also promised I believe a supplemental report from Dr. Tabeau, who is a demographer, who testified a week or so prior to the break. We have not -- although I spoke briefly with my learned friend about that, I just want to put it on the table so that we continue to follow up on that issue. I'm not sure what the time frame is for us to receive that report, although we were hoping we would receive it at least by today if not prior to our arrival here this week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No doubt that we all have some problems seeing 65 ter numbers 77, this is Ms. Ewa Tabeau and Mr. Inayat. I'm afraid this will take a lot of time when I anticipate your questions. So therefore, it should also be taken into account. I think it would be really helpful if the OTP could, as soon as possible, provide all of us with a time schedule until the 19th of September that we all know what we can expect during this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: We can provide a schedule of those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Provisional, no doubt. The unexpected will happen. Any additional?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: One last point, Your Honour, respectfully this is not a criticism, it is an attempt to have a clarification in connection with the revised scheduling order that we have dated August 2nd of this year. If I may just be permitted to put it in context, the witnesses that the OTP is planning to call now certainly seem to be those witnesses that are not fact witnesses but opinion witnesses, some which we will object to as being so-called expert witnesses. It is for those witnesses in particular Your Honour that I believe the Defence needs to meet with Dr. Stakic to go over the materials in detail. The schedule respectfully as proposed does not give the Defence attorneys an opportunity to visit Dr. Stakic in the Detention Centre in order to go over those materials. And again, I understand we don't have it all in the language in which Dr. Stakic would understand, namely Serbian or B/C/S as it's referred to, but we would also if the witness testifies, and we most certainly appreciate the Court's indulgence, today, for example, by giving us an opportunity to further clarify issues and questions for the witness tomorrow. If we may from time to time be permitted to ask the Court to take a break or to recommence or reconvene questioning at a subsequent time so that we would be given an opportunity to discuss it with Dr. Stakic. As the Court knows, the Detention Unit does not allow us to have weekend visits and does not permit us to go there after I believe 5 or 5.30. So we're kind of constrained with that -- 4.30. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: No doubt, this is one of the purposes that we envisaged to have morning and afternoon sessions that will hopefully allow us to cancel the one or other afternoon session and we'll give you the opportunity. Maybe it's necessary, then please ask one or two days beforehand that for a special witness, you need special preparation that we can fix this date in a special way. We are flexible, and the schedule until Thursday, 19 September, is envisaged to have this flexibility for both parties because I know it's for you difficult to discuss it with your client. It's for the OTP difficult to summon the witnesses during this very short period of time. So if we could have this provisional schedule from the OTP, this would enlighten us to a certain extent and give you the basis to say before we hear this witness, we have to discuss the issue with our client.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Any other issues? This is not the case. The trial then stays adjourned until tomorrow, 10.00. Please, 10.00, because there is another Status Conference in front of the hearing. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
